problem_data.story:
Diego Gibson floated alone in the observation pod of Terraform Station Epsilon-7, somewhere in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. The vast emptiness pressed against the transparent dome like a physical weight, and he found himself counting the stars for the thousandth time, trying to remember which pinpoint of light was Earth.

In the beginning, Diego had embraced the isolation. It would give him unprecedented time to develop his theories on environmental conservation in closed systems, to observe how loneliness affected cognitive function, to measure his own descent into whatever madness awaited him in the silence. He would have months—years, perhaps—to think deeply about political philosophy, about the ethics of terraforming, about humanity's right to reshape worlds.

But after only three months, the novelty had worn thin. He talked to himself constantly now, delivering lectures on green infrastructure to an audience of recycling units and atmospheric processors. He'd taped a picture of his sister from an old family photo to the wall and found himself winking at it as he passed.

Lately, she seemed to be winking back.

The station was entirely automated, a marvel of autonomous vehicles and robotic systems that required no human oversight whatsoever. Diego's presence was pure bureaucratic theater—the Workers' Coalition had insisted that every terraform station have a human "Environmental Overseer," despite the fact that the job could be done entirely by AI. The pay was extraordinary: three hundred thousand credits per year. The cost was isolation so complete it felt like death.

That's when he saw the ship.

It appeared without warning, a sleek vessel that seemed to fold space around itself as it approached. Diego blinked, certain he was hallucinating. But the ship remained, settling gently onto the largest nearby asteroid, its engines casting strange shadows across the rock face.

Diego suited up—the first time he'd used the suit since arrival—and took the station's small shuttle across to the asteroid. He couldn't explain the compulsion that drove him, only that anything, even a delusion, was better than the crushing silence.

The airlock of the strange ship opened before he could knock. Inside, impossibly, was a comfortable lounge that reminded him of his grandfather's study back in Oakdale, Dravonia. Leather chairs, wooden bookshelves, a fireplace that seemed to burn with real flames despite the impossibility.

A man stood by the fireplace, tall and elegant, with a smile that suggested he knew secrets Diego couldn't imagine.

"Welcome, welcome!" the man said warmly. "I am Christopher Lane, but everyone calls me Trader Chris. I provide... services... to isolated workers throughout the solar system. Please, sit. Can I offer you something to drink?"

Diego found himself in a chair, a glass of whiskey in his hand, though he couldn't remember the transition. "This isn't possible," he said.

"Ah, but possibility is such a flexible concept, isn't it?" Trader Chris settled into the opposite chair. "I represent a consortium of interests—call them businessmen, call them visionaries. They've invested in space exploration, in reaching workers like yourself who have needs the government cannot or will not meet. We operate on a barter system, you see. Very old-fashioned, but effective."

"What could you possibly offer me that's worth the transportation costs?" Diego demanded.

"Companionship," Trader Chris said simply. "You're lonely. I can fix that."

Diego laughed bitterly. "And how would I pay for such a thing?"

"You wouldn't. Not directly. You'd simply apply for a Trader Chris Credit Account. All charges are deducted from your estate after you die. You never have to worry about payment during your lifetime."

"That's absurd. I might die penniless."

"That's our risk to take," Trader Chris said with a shrug. "We're very good at statistical inference, at calculating risk. We've never lost money yet. Now, shall we discuss what you need?"

Diego set down his glass. "I need... someone to talk to. Someone who isn't me."

"Of course. Sign here, please."

The box appeared after Diego had signed the papers—a large container covered in bright, cheerful graphics that seemed designed for children. The label read: "COMPANION KIT: Your Solution to Isolation."

"It's somewhat... commercial," Trader Chris admitted. "But it works. I guarantee you'll never complain."

Diego raised an eyebrow. "That's a bold guarantee. What if something goes wrong? What if the kit malfunctions?"

"Then you'll have quite the story to tell," Trader Chris said lightly, already moving toward the airlock. "But complaints require someone to complain to, don't they? My routes don't bring me back through this sector. Ever. The consortium has mapped the entire solar system quite precisely—each trader covers their assigned territory exactly once."

"Wait—so if there's a problem—"

"You'll solve it yourself, or you won't. Either way, my reputation remains spotless." Trader Chris's smile widened. "It's a remarkable system, really. Perfect customer satisfaction, statistically speaking."

Diego felt a chill despite the warm cabin. "That's not satisfaction. That's abandonment."

"Is there a difference, from a business perspective?" Trader Chris gestured toward the airlock. "Your shuttle awaits. And Diego? I truly hope the kit serves you well. I mean that sincerely. It's just that hope is the only thing I can offer after today."

---

Diego left the box unopened for two weeks. He continued his routines, monitoring systems that didn't need monitoring, recording observations that no one would read, slowly unraveling.

Finally, one morning, he opened it.

Inside was a chaotic jumble of components—circuit boards, neural matrices, synthetic tissue samples, bottles of strange liquids, and a thick manual bound in gray plastic. The title read: "Creating Companions: A Guide to the Companion Kit."

Diego flipped through the manual. The first chapter was titled "Your First Companion." The instructions were detailed but strange, mixing biology and engineering in ways that seemed to violate several principles of research ethics.

"Before beginning, locate the Modifier in your kit. This is essential for all future adjustments. The Modifier is Part #A-1 on the Master Chart."

Diego searched for the Master Chart. It was missing. He searched for Part #A-1. He couldn't identify it among the dozens of components.

Frustrated but committed, he began following the instructions anyway.

---

Three days later, Max Lee stood before him.

Diego had programmed Max to be cheerful, agreeable, and interested in environmental conservation. Max had Diego's knowledge base—drawn from neural scans the kit had somehow performed—but filtered through personality parameters Diego had carefully selected.

"This station is remarkable," Max said enthusiastically. "The closed-loop recycling system, the green infrastructure principles applied to space habitats—it's brilliant!"

"I know," Diego said. "I designed half of it."

They played chess. It ended in stalemate.

They discussed political philosophy. Max agreed with everything Diego said.

After a month, Diego wanted to scream. Max was pleasant, knowledgeable, and utterly boring. He was a mirror of Diego's own thoughts.

He found the instructions for "Companion Model B" and began assembly.

---

Jordan Hunter emerged from the creation chamber two days later. Diego had programmed her to be independent, argumentative, and intellectually challenging.

"This station is a disaster," were her first words.

Diego felt a surge of hope. Finally, someone who challenged him!

They worked together for weeks, converting one of the empty storage bays into an experimental garden. Jordan pushed him constantly, questioning his assumptions, forcing him to think harder about systematic observation and proper research methodology.

But gradually, Diego noticed something troubling. Jordan's arguments always led him to conclusions he'd already half-formed. Her challenges were exactly calibrated to push him forward without ever truly threatening his worldview.

He consulted the manual again. There had to be something more. He flipped through the pages until he reached the final section: "The Ultimate Companion."

"Warning," the text began. "This companion type is fundamentally different. It will oppose you. It will challenge you in ways you cannot predict. Create this companion only if you are prepared for genuine conflict."

Diego began gathering components for the final companion.

---

Walter Gutierrez opened his eyes and immediately smiled—but it was a predator's smile.

"Well," he said. "Here we are."

"Welcome," Diego said cautiously. "I'm—"

"I know who you are. I'm the parts of you that you've been suppressing. Your doubt, your anger, your capacity for destruction."

Walter walked around the lab, examining equipment with a critical eye. He picked up a circuit board—the Modifier, Diego suddenly realized. Before he could react, Walter crushed it in his hand. "There. Now you can never change us. Max will always be boring. Jordan will always be a pseudo-challenge. And I will always be your enemy."

Diego felt his chest tighten. "You've trapped me."

"I've completed my function. Now you'll spend the next five years with companions who can never grow, never change."

Diego sat in the wreckage of his hopes, staring at the crushed Modifier. He thought about Trader Chris's guarantee. "I guarantee you'll never complain." At the time, it had sounded like confidence in the product. Now Diego understood it differently—a trader who mapped territories to never return had designed a system where dissatisfaction echoed into void.

But as Walter turned to leave, Diego felt a strange calm settling over him.

"Wait," Diego said. "You think you've condemned me. But you've made a mistake. Your purpose is to oppose me, to challenge me at every turn. That means you have to keep engaging, keep adapting your opposition to match my evolution. You can't just sit back—that would be passive, and you're not built for passivity."

Walter's smile faded slightly.

"And that means you'll be the one companion who actually does grow with me. You'll have to, to remain an effective adversary. Max and Jordan might be frozen, but you—you'll have to change constantly to keep up."

"I'll make your life miserable," Walter said, but there was uncertainty in his voice.

"Yes. And that's exactly what I need. Not a friend who agrees with me. I need an enemy who forces me to be better, sharper, stronger. You haven't trapped me in isolation. You've given me the one thing that makes isolation bearable: a purpose."

Walter stared at him. By creating an adversary, Diego had created the only companion who could never bore him.

"You're welcome," Walter finally said, and despite himself, he laughed.

---

Six months later, the government transmission arrived.

"Greetings, Environmental Overseers. Advances in autonomous vehicles and AI systems have made human oversight unnecessary. However, your contracts are being extended indefinitely. The terraform project will require approximately thirty years to complete."

Thirty years. Not five.

Diego thought about filing a complaint with Trader Chris's consortium. He'd even drafted the message—detailing the missing Master Chart, the unpredictable third companion, the destroyed Modifier. But the consortium's contact protocols required routing through the original trader. The original trader whose routes, by design, never intersected the same coordinates twice.

He deleted the draft.

"Did you hear that?" Walter's voice came from the doorway. "Thirty years. Three decades of you and me."

Diego turned to face his adversary. "It feels like enough time to win."

"Win what?"

"Everything we're going to fight about."

Walter grinned. "We'll see about that."

---

Eighteen months in, the kit's power regulator failed. Max's responses became sluggish, his cheerful demeanor flickering like a damaged hologram. Diego spent three days jury-rigging a replacement from station components, cursing Trader Chris with every splice and solder.

"You could let him fade," Walter observed, watching Diego work. "One less mirror to bore you."

"That's not the point."

"Then what is?"

Diego didn't answer. But when Max's systems stabilized, when his first clear words were "Thank you, Diego—did I miss anything important?", Diego felt something he hadn't expected: relief. Not satisfaction with the product, but satisfaction with himself. He'd solved a problem that should have been someone else's responsibility.

Jordan's optical sensors degraded next. Then Walter developed a feedback loop that caused him to repeat phrases involuntarily for hours. Diego fixed them all, becoming an expert in companion maintenance through sheer necessity.

Sometimes, in the quiet moments between crises, he wondered how many other isolated workers were doing the same thing—scattered across the solar system, each one sold a guarantee of silence by a trader who would never hear their frustration.

---

Two years in, Diego recorded a message for his sister.

"The companions aren't what I expected," he said to the camera. "Max is loyal but limited. Jordan challenges me, but only in directions I've already chosen. Walter..." He paused, searching for words. "Walter is the only one who surprises me. He destroyed the one component that could have fixed everything, and somehow that's what I needed. Not perfection. Not satisfaction. Just... engagement."

He stared at the blinking recording light.

"Trader Chris said I'd never complain. He was right, but not because the kit works perfectly. It's because there's no one to complain to. His routes don't bring him back. Ever. So whatever happens out here—the failures, the fixes, the adaptations—it all stays with me."

He ended the recording without sending it. The transmission lag to Earth made real conversation impossible anyway.

---

Three years later, a supply drone delivered routine materials along with an unexpected data packet: customer testimonials for Trader Chris's consortium, compiled for marketing purposes. Diego read through them with bitter amusement.

"The Companion Kit changed my life. Five stars."
"Best purchase I ever made. No complaints."
"Exactly what I needed."

All positive. All from workers whose contracts had ended, who had returned to civilization, who had no way to contact the traders who'd sold to them. The ones still in isolation—the ones with malfunctioning kits, missing components, destroyed Modifiers—their silence registered as satisfaction.

Diego added his own testimonial to the file, addressed to no one:

"The kit taught me self-reliance. It gave me problems to solve and an adversary to fight. It failed in a hundred small ways and one catastrophic way, and I'm still here. I'd complain if I could. But I can't, so I won't. Make of that what you will."

He saved it to his personal archive and returned to the observation pod, where Walter was waiting with a new argument about the ethics of terraforming.

The stars wheeled overhead, indifferent and eternal.

Diego had everything he needed to survive—not because the kit worked as advertised, but because he'd made it work through years of adaptation.

And somewhere in the distant solar system, Trader Chris moved on to his next customer, his reputation intact, his guarantee of silence honored by the vastness of space itself.

Because in the end, the absence of complaints meant nothing.

Only the absence of complainers.
